value.overview: The Blue-gray Tanager is a common, conspicuous songbird of tropical America. Its soft blue-gray body and brighter blue wings make it readily recognizable in gardens, plantations, forest edges, and towns. Adaptable and often comfortable near people, it usually occurs in pairs or small groups and regularly visits fruiting trees and feeders. Fruit forms much of its diet, supplemented by insects, nectar, and other plant material.
value.classification: The Blue-gray Tanager, Thraupis episcopus, belongs to the tanager family Thraupidae within the order Passeriformes. Numerous geographic subspecies are recognized across its broad range.
value.identification: This medium-sized tanager measures about 16–18 cm long and has a compact body, rounded head, and short, fairly thick bill. Adults are mostly pale blue-gray, becoming brighter blue on the wings and tail. The shoulders may appear deep blue or whitish depending on the subspecies. Males and females look alike, although males may average slightly brighter. Juveniles are generally duller and grayer than adults. Its pale body distinguishes it from darker, browner Palm Tanagers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America, including Trinidad and Tobago. In Costa Rica it is a very common resident in tropical and subtropical lowlands and foothills, especially around forest edges, secondary growth, plantations, gardens, parks, towns, and fruit feeders. It generally avoids the interior of dense, unbroken forest and benefits from landscapes containing scattered trees, shrubs, and fruiting vegetation.
value.migrationStatus: Primarily a nonmigratory resident. Individuals may make short local or seasonal movements in response to food availability.
value.breeding: Breeding timing varies geographically and may follow local rainfall and food cycles. The female builds a compact, open cup nest from plant fibers, grasses, roots, and similar material, placing it in a tree, shrub, palm, or occasionally on a human-made structure. A typical clutch contains one to three eggs. The female performs most or all incubation for roughly two weeks, while both parents generally help feed the nestlings. Pairs may remain together beyond the breeding season.
value.dietFeeding: Blue-gray Tanagers feed mainly on fruits and berries, often taking small fruits whole or tearing pieces from larger ones while perched. They also consume insects and other small invertebrates, nectar, flower parts, and occasionally cultivated foods. Foraging takes place chiefly in shrubs and trees, including the canopy, but the birds readily visit gardens and feeding stations. Their fruit-eating habits help disperse seeds through disturbed and regenerating habitats.
value.behavior: Usually seen in pairs, family parties, or small groups, Blue-gray Tanagers may also join mixed-species feeding flocks or gather at abundant fruit sources. They are active, alert birds that move through exposed branches and foliage while searching for food. Pairs can defend nesting areas and may behave aggressively toward other birds at feeders or fruiting trees. Their vocalizations include thin, squeaky calls and a simple, rambling song rather than a rich musical performance.

conservation.status: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List; the species has a very large range and remains common in many areas.
conservation.populationTrend: Increasing; the global population has not been precisely quantified, but the species is widespread, adaptable, and often prospers in human-modified habitats.
